title: Why Astronauts Get Constipated in Space — Scientists Finally Know
summary:
Have you ever wondered why astronauts complain about constipation? Scientists just found a clue — and it's all about what happens inside your gut when gravity disappears.

Researchers from the University of Copenhagen, working with NASA, studied blood samples from 52 astronauts who spent months on the International Space Station. They found that within weeks of arriving in space, the astronauts' gut bacteria started breaking down protein more than usual. This process is called protein fermentation.

Normally, bacteria in your intestines eat fiber from food. But in space, something changes. The researchers think microgravity — the almost-weightless feeling in orbit — slows down how fast food moves through the digestive tract. If food stays in the intestines longer, bacteria run out of fiber and start fermenting protein instead.

'We see changes in astronauts' blood samples that indicate that the gut bacteria begin to ferment protein to a greater extent than usual within weeks after the astronauts arrive in space,' says Giorgia La Barbera, one of the study's lead authors.

That matters because protein fermentation can produce substances linked to health problems, like kidney damage and even effects on mood or focus. The changes continued until the astronauts returned to Earth.

So what can be done? The team suggests eating more fiber, taking prebiotics, or using treatments that help food move through the gut faster. These ideas could help astronauts on long missions to the Moon or Mars — and maybe even help people with digestive problems here on Earth.
why_it_matters: Your gut bacteria help keep you healthy, so learning what makes them change far from Earth can also teach doctors how to help people with stomach problems right here at home.

background_read: The International Space Station (a huge laboratory orbiting Earth, where astronauts from many countries live and work for months at a time) has had people on board continuously since 2000.
NASA (the U.S. space agency) worked with the University of Copenhagen (a famous university in Denmark) on this study.

Gravity is the force that pulls everything toward Earth. Astronauts on the space station float because they are falling around the planet — that nearly weightless state is what scientists call microgravity.
Article_Structure: WHO: Researchers from the University of Copenhagen working with NASA, and 52 astronauts who lived on the International Space Station.
WHAT: They found that astronauts' gut bacteria start fermenting protein within weeks of arriving in space.
WHERE: Samples came from astronauts in orbit on the International Space Station, and were analyzed back on Earth.
WHY: Because microgravity seems to slow food down in the intestines, leaving bacteria without fiber, which may harm health — so scientists want fixes like more fiber and prebiotics.

perspectives.description: The findings could help astronauts stay healthy on long trips to the Moon or Mars — and might lead to new treatments for people on Earth.
Only 52 astronauts were studied and only their blood was tested, so scientists cannot be fully sure what is happening inside their guts.
Space changes the human body in many ways, and this is one more example of how living without gravity pushes the body into unusual patterns.
